relationship: parallel prophetic dating under the same Judean kings
rationale: Isaiah and Hosea both date their prophetic revelation under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, using the respective supplied name forms. Hosea additionally names Israel's Jeroboam.
source_text: The vision that Isaiah son of Amos saw, which he saw against Judea and against Jerusalem during the reign of Oziah, Joatham, Achaz and Hezekiah, who reigned over Judea.

target_units.text: The word of the Lord that came to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel.

relationship: close heavenly-earthly summons and unfaithful children
rationale: Both summon heaven and earth to hear before describing Israel as children who fail their divine Father. Isaiah speaks of sons raised high who reject Him; Deuteronomy calls the generation blemished and asks how it repays the Father who made it.
source_text: Listen, heaven, and give ear, earth, because the Lord has spoken: “I begot sons and raised them high, but they rejected Me.

target_units.text: Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth.
Let my utterance be awaited as the rain, and let my words descend as the dew, as a shower upon the grass, and as snow upon the herbage.
For I have called upon the name of the Lord; ascribe greatness unto our God.
God—true are His works, and all His ways are judgments; a faithful God, and there is no unrighteousness; righteous and holy is the Lord.
Blemished children, not His, have sinned—a crooked and perverse generation.
Do you thus repay the Lord, O foolish people and unwise? Is not He Himself your Father, who acquired you, and made you, and created you?

relationship: close animals knowing what God's people do not
rationale: Isaiah contrasts an ox knowing its owner and a donkey its master's manger with Israel's failure to know God; Jeremiah contrasts birds observing their appointed times with the people's ignorance of the Lord's judgments. The animals and the knowledge specified differ.
source_text: An ox knew the one who acquired it, and a donkey its lord’s manger; but Israel did not know Me, and the people did not understand Me.”

target_units.text: Even the stork in heaven knew her time; turtledove and swallow, field sparrows, kept the times of their coming, but My people did not know the Lord’s judgments.

relationship: close abandonment of the divine Father and provocation
rationale: Isaiah indicts lawless sons for abandoning the Lord and provoking Him; Deuteronomy likewise describes Israel forsaking the God who begot and nourished it and provoking Him through unfaithfulness.
source_text: Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins, evil offspring, lawless sons! You abandoned the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger.

target_units.text: And Jacob ate and was filled, and the beloved one kicked; he grew fat, he grew thick, he grew broad; and he forsook God who made him, and departed from God his Saviour.
They provoked Me with foreign gods; with their abominations they embittered Me.
They sacrificed unto demons, and not unto God, unto gods whom they did not know; new ones, lately come, whom their fathers did not know.
You forsook God who begat you, and forgot God who nourishes you.
And the Lord saw, and was jealous, and was provoked by the anger of His sons and daughters.
And He said, I will turn My face from them, and show what shall befall them at the last; for they are a perverse generation, sons in whom is no faithfulness.

relationship: parallel punishment failing to produce correction
rationale: Isaiah asks why further blows should fall as lawlessness increases; Jeremiah says the scourged people refuse instruction and harden themselves instead of returning. Neither presents the blows as having secured repentance.
source_text: Why should you be struck again as you add lawlessness? Every head is in pain, and every heart in grief.

target_units.text: Lord, Thine eyes are toward faithfulness. Thou didst scourge them, and they did not suffer; Thou broughtest them to an end, and they would not accept instruction. They hardened their faces beyond rock and would not return.

relationship: related untreated injury as a figure for the people
rationale: Isaiah describes wounds without poultice, oil or bandages; Jeremiah likewise depicts the people's fracture being treated with contempt by those announcing peace. The latter specifies misleading religious leaders rather than Isaiah's catalogue of untreated injuries.
source_text: From feet to head: for neither a wound nor a bruise nor an inflamed blow is there a poultice to apply, nor oil nor bandages.

target_units.text: For from their small to their great, all have carried out lawless deeds; from priest to false prophet, all have done false things.
And they treated My people’s fracture with contempt, saying, ‘Peace, peace’; and where is peace?

relationship: covenant-judgment counterpart to devastated land and cities
rationale: Isaiah describes deserted land, burned cities and foreign consumption; Leviticus threatens desolated cities and land, enemies dwelling there and scattering among nations. Burning and consumption are Isaiah's particular details.
source_text: Your land is deserted, your cities burned by fire. Your country—foreigners consume it before you; it has been deserted, overturned by foreign peoples.

target_units.text: and I will make your cities desolate, and lay waste your holy places; and I will in no wise smell the savour of your sacrifices;
and I Myself will desolate your land, and your enemies who dwell in it shall marvel at it.
And I will scatter you among the nations, and the advancing sword shall consume you. Your land shall become desolate, and your cities shall be desolate.

relationship: internal repeated fruit-watcher shelter image
rationale: Isaiah 1 compares isolated Daughter Zion to a fruit-watcher's shelter; Isaiah 24 compares the shaken earth to the same kind of shelter. The fragile rural structure depicts distinct scales of devastation.
source_text: Daughter Zion will be left like a tent in a vineyard, like a fruit-watcher’s shelter in a cucumber field, like a besieged city.

target_units.text: The earth has tilted and will be shaken like a fruit-watcher’s shelter, like someone drunk and hungover. It will fall and will never be able to rise, for lawlessness has prevailed upon it.

relationship: explicit quotation of the preserved seed and Sodom comparison
rationale: Romans expressly introduces Isaiah's words and repeats that without the Lord Sabaoth leaving seed, the people would have become like Sodom and Gomorrah.
source_text: If the Lord Sabaoth had not left us seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.

target_units.text: And just as Isaiah has said beforehand, “Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah.”

relationship: parallel prophetic comparison of Jerusalem with Sodom
rationale: Isaiah addresses Jerusalem's rulers and people under Sodom and Gomorrah's names; Ezekiel calls Sodom Jerusalem's sister and says Jerusalem surpassed her lawlessness. These are moral comparisons, not a claim that the cities are geographically identical.
source_text: Hear the Lord’s word, rulers of Sodom! Attend to God’s law, people of Gomorrah!

target_units.text: Your elder sister is Samaria, she and her daughters, dwelling at your left; your sister younger than you, dwelling at your right, is Sodom and her daughters.
Not even so did you walk in their ways or act according to their lawlessness. Before long, you surpass them in all your ways.
As I live, says the Lord, your sister Sodom, she and her daughters, certainly did not do as you and your daughters have done.

Yet this was the lawlessness of your sister Sodom: arrogance. In fullness of bread and abundance of wine she and her daughters lived luxuriously. This belonged to her and her daughters, but they did not support the hand of the poor and needy.
They boasted greatly and committed acts of lawlessness before Me, and I removed them as I saw.

relationship: close divine rejection of reliance on sacrificial animals
rationale: Isaiah says the Lord does not desire the abundance of rams, bulls' blood and goats; the psalm likewise refuses calves and goats and asks whether God eats bulls' flesh or drinks goats' blood. Their respective arguments challenge dependence on the offerings themselves.
source_text: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to Me?” says the Lord. “I am full of burnt offerings of rams; fat of lambs and blood of bulls and male goats I do not desire,

target_units.text: I will not rebuke you concerning your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are continually before Me.
I will not receive calves from your house or young goats from your flocks.
For all the forest’s wild animals are Mine, beasts on the mountains and cattle.
I know all the birds of heaven, and the field’s beauty is with Me.
If I become hungry, I will certainly not tell you, for the inhabited world and its fullness are Mine.
Will I eat bulls’ flesh or drink goats’ blood?

relationship: parallel questioning of what worship the Lord seeks
rationale: Isaiah asks who demanded the worshipers' coming and trampling of His court; Micah asks whether offerings secure approach to God and answers with justice, mercy and readiness to walk with Him. Isaiah's surrounding summons to ethical reform supplies the comparable setting.
source_text: not even if you come to appear before Me. For who demanded these things from your hands? To trample My court,

target_units.text: With what shall I take hold of the Lord and grasp my God Most High? Shall I take hold of Him with whole burnt offerings, with year-old calves?
Will the Lord receive with thousands of rams or with ten thousands of fat-rich torrents? Shall I give my firstborn offspring for impieties, the fruit of my body for the sin of my life?
Has it been declared to you, O man, what is good? Or what does the Lord seek from you, except to do justice, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?

relationship: close rejected festivals offerings and ritual sounds
rationale: Isaiah calls flour offerings futile and incense abominable and refuses the named observances; Amos likewise rejects festivals and offerings and refuses to hear their music. Their lists overlap in rejected ritual rather than every individual item.
source_text: you will no longer continue. If you bring fine flour, it is futile. Incense is an abomination to Me. Your new moons and sabbaths and a great day I cannot endure; fasting and idleness,

target_units.text: “I have hated and rejected your festivals, and I certainly will not smell a pleasing scent in your festal gatherings,
because even if you bring Me whole burnt offerings and your sacrifices, I will not receive them, and I will not look upon the salvation offering of your display.
Remove from Me the sound of your songs; I will not listen to the music of your instruments,

relationship: close divine hatred of the people's festivals
rationale: Both directly state the Lord's hatred or rejection of the people's festivals. Isaiah additionally names new moons and refuses to continue overlooking their sins.
source_text: and your new moons and your festivals My soul hates. You have become more than enough for Me; I will no longer let your sins go.

target_units.text: “I have hated and rejected your festivals, and I certainly will not smell a pleasing scent in your festal gatherings,

relationship: internal bloodstained hands and withdrawn divine attention
rationale: Isaiah 1 joins unanswered prayer and God's turned-away eyes with hands full of blood; Isaiah 59 likewise joins God's turned-away face with offenses and hands stained by blood. The latter explains that the barrier is sin, not inability to hear or save.
source_text: Whenever you stretch your hands toward Me, I will turn My eyes away from you. Even if you multiply supplication, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood.

target_units.text: Is the Lord’s hand unable to save? Or has His ear grown heavy so that He cannot hear?
Instead, your offenses stand between you and God, and because of your sins He has turned His face away from you so as not to show mercy.
For your hands are stained with blood and your fingers with sins. Your lips spoke lawlessness, and your tongue meditates on injustice.

relationship: close cleansing of hands hearts and conduct
rationale: Isaiah summons the people to wash, remove evils from their souls and stop evil deeds; James likewise commands sinners to cleanse their hands and purify their hearts as they draw near to God.
source_text: Wash yourselves, become clean. Remove the evils from your souls, before My eyes. Stop your evil deeds.

target_units.text: Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, sinners, and purify your hearts, you of divided mind.

relationship: close justice for the wronged orphan and widow
rationale: Both command justice and rescue of the wronged and expressly protect orphans and widows. Jeremiah additionally names the newcomer and prohibits innocent bloodshed.
source_text: Learn to do good, seek judgment, rescue the wronged. Give judgment for the orphan and vindicate the widow.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Do justice and righteousness; rescue the plundered from the hand of the one wronging him. Do not oppress the newcomer, orphan, or widow, and do not act impiously or shed innocent blood in this place.

relationship: close cleansing from sin expressed through whiteness and snow
rationale: Isaiah promises that deeply colored sins will be whitened like snow and wool; the psalmist likewise expects divine washing to make him whiter than snow. Wool and the purple-red and scarlet colors belong to Isaiah.
source_text: Come, let us reason together, says the Lord. Though your sins are like purple-red, I will whiten them like snow; though they are like scarlet, I will whiten them like wool.

target_units.text: Thou wilt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I will be cleansed; Thou wilt wash me, and I will be whitened beyond snow.

relationship: covenant blessing of obedient enjoyment of the land
rationale: Isaiah promises the land's good things to willing hearers; Leviticus likewise links keeping God's commandments to the land's produce and eating bread to satisfaction.
source_text: If you are willing and listen to Me, you will eat the land’s good things.

target_units.text: If you walk in My ordinances, keep My commandments, and do them,
then I will give you rain in its season. The land shall yield its produce, and the trees of the fields shall yield their fruit.
And your threshing shall reach the grape harvest, and the grape harvest shall reach the sowing. You shall eat your bread to satisfaction and dwell securely in your land.

relationship: covenant penalty of the sword after refusal to obey
rationale: Isaiah warns that the sword will devour those unwilling to listen; Leviticus likewise threatens a covenant-avenging sword when the people resist correction and persist in crooked conduct.
source_text: But if you are unwilling and do not listen to Me, a sword will devour you, for the Lord’s mouth has spoken these things.”

target_units.text: And if by these things you are not disciplined, but walk crookedly toward Me,
then I too will walk with you in contrary anger, and I too will strike you seven times in return for your sins.
And I will bring upon you a sword exacting the penalty of the covenant. You shall flee into your cities, and I will send death among you; you shall be handed into enemies’ hands.

relationship: parallel Jerusalem portrayed as an unfaithful woman
rationale: Isaiah contrasts formerly faithful and righteous Zion with a prostitute and murderers; Ezekiel likewise describes Jerusalem brought into God's covenant and then prostituting herself through trust in her beauty. The accounts develop different details of the city's betrayal.
source_text: How the faithful city Zion has become a prostitute, full of judgment, in which righteousness lay at rest, but now murderers!

target_units.text: I passed through you and saw you; behold, your season was the season of those lodging. I spread My wings over you and covered your exposure. I swore to you and entered a covenant with you, says the Lord, and you became Mine.
I washed you with water, washed your blood off you, and anointed you with oil,
and clothed you in patterned garments, gave you blue-purple footwear, girded you with fine linen, and wrapped you in hair-woven cloth,
and adorned you with ornaments, placed bracelets around your hands and a necklace around your neck,
and put a ring around your nostril, little hoops upon your ears and a crown of boasting upon your head.
You were adorned with gold and silver; your coverings were fine linen, hair-woven and patterned. You ate fine flour, oil and honey, and became very beautiful.
Your fame went out among the nations because of your beauty, for it was made complete in splendor, in the loveliness I placed upon you, says the Lord.
You trusted in your beauty and prostituted yourself because of your fame. You poured out your prostitution upon every passerby—which will not be.

relationship: close rejected silver as a figure for corruption
rationale: Isaiah calls the city's silver unapproved; Jeremiah calls the corrupt people rejected silver because wickedness was not melted away and the Lord rejected them. Isaiah's diluted wine is a separate accompanying image.
source_text: Your silver is unapproved; your retailers mix the wine with water.

target_units.text: All are unheeding, walking crookedly, bronze and iron; all are corrupted.
The bellows failed from the fire; the lead failed. In vain the silversmith works silver; their wickedness was not melted away.
Call them rejected silver, because the Lord rejected them.

relationship: contrast between corrupt rulers and God's impartial justice
rationale: Isaiah's rulers love gifts and neglect orphans and widows; Deuteronomy describes God as taking no bribe and executing judgment for the orphan and widow. The rulers contradict the particular judicial qualities attributed to God.
source_text: Your rulers disobey, partners of thieves, loving gifts and pursuing repayment, not judging for orphans and not attending to widows’ judgment.

target_units.text: For the Lord your God, He is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great and mighty and fearful God, who shows no partiality, neither takes a bribe;
who executes judgment for the sojourner, and the orphan, and the widow, and loves the sojourner, to give him bread and clothing.

relationship: close divine repayment of enemies through judgment
rationale: Isaiah announces the Lord's judgment against His enemies; Deuteronomy likewise joins God's hand taking hold of judgment with repayment to enemies and those who hate Him.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Master, the Lord Sabaoth: “Woe, mighty ones of Israel! For My anger will not cease among My opponents, and I will exact judgment from My enemies.

target_units.text: For I will sharpen My sword as lightning, and My hand shall lay hold of judgment; and I will repay a penalty unto the enemies, and unto them that hate Me will I repay.
I will make My arrows drunk with blood, and My sword shall devour flesh, from the blood of the slain and of captives, from the head of the rulers of the enemies.

Rejoice, O heavens, together with Him, and let all the sons of God worship Him; rejoice, O nations, with His people, and let all the angels of God give Him strength; for He avenges the blood of His sons, and shall avenge and repay a penalty unto the enemies, and unto them that hate Him shall He repay; and the Lord shall thoroughly cleanse the land of His people.

relationship: parallel divine purification by burning and refining
rationale: Isaiah promises to burn the city to purity and remove lawless people; Malachi depicts the Lord's arrival as a smelting fire that purifies Levi's sons like precious metal. City and priestly group are distinct objects of purification.
source_text: I will bring My hand against you and burn you to purity. I will destroy the disobedient, remove all lawless people from you and humble all the arrogant.

target_units.text: And who will endure the day of his entrance? Or who will stand at his appearance? For he enters like a smelting fire and like launderers’ herb.

He will sit, smelting and purifying as with silver and gold. He will cleanse the sons of Levi and melt them like gold and silver, and they will be those who bring a sacrifice to the Lord in righteousness.

relationship: close renewed Jerusalem receiving a faithful name
rationale: Isaiah promises restored judges and the name City of Righteousness, Faithful Metropolis Zion; Zechariah likewise promises God's return to Jerusalem and its designation as the True City and His mountain as holy.
source_text: I will establish your judges as before and your counselors as at the beginning. After these things you will be called City of Righteousness, Faithful Metropolis Zion.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: I will return to Zion and dwell within Jerusalem. Jerusalem will be called the True City, and the mountain of the Lord Almighty a Holy Mountain.

relationship: parallel mercy and salvation for Judah
rationale: Isaiah says Zion's captivity will be saved through judgment and mercy; Hosea likewise promises mercy and salvation to Judah's sons through the Lord their God. Hosea does not repeat Isaiah's captivity-and-judgment formulation.
source_text: For her captivity will be saved through judgment and through mercy.

target_units.text: But I will show mercy to Judah’s sons and save them by the Lord their God. I will not save them by bow, sword, war, chariots, horses or horsemen.”

relationship: close collective destruction of the lawless
rationale: Isaiah says lawless people and sinners will be shattered together; the psalm likewise says the lawless will be destroyed together and the ungodly remnant destroyed.
source_text: The lawless and sinners will be shattered together, and those abandoning the Lord will be brought to an end.

target_units.text: But the lawless will be destroyed together; the remnants of the ungodly will be destroyed.

relationship: internal gardens associated with provocative worship
rationale: Isaiah 1 joins shame over desired idols and gardens; Isaiah 65 explicitly describes sacrifices in gardens among practices that provoke God. The later passage clarifies a comparable illicit use of gardens without identifying a particular garden here.
source_text: For they will be ashamed of their idols, which they themselves wanted, and they were disgraced by their gardens, which they desired.

target_units.text: This people continually provokes Me to My face. They sacrifice in gardens and burn incense on bricks to demons that do not exist,

relationship: parallel waterless growth picturing the ungodly's failure
rationale: Isaiah compares the judged people to a leafless tree and a waterless garden; Bildad likewise asks whether wetland plants grow without water before applying their failure to those forgetting the Lord. Plant species and the speaker's immediate setting differ.
source_text: For they will be like a terebinth that has shed its leaves, like a garden that has no water.

target_units.text: Does papyrus flourish without water, or will a rush grow tall without a drink?
While it is still on its root and unharvested, does not every plant wither before it drinks?
So, then, will be the latter end of all who forget the Lord; for the hope of an ungodly person will perish.

relationship: parallel combustible growth and unquenchable judgment
rationale: Isaiah makes strength a stalk of tow and works sparks of fire and says lawless people burn with no quencher; John the Baptist likewise uses rejected trees and chaff for judgment and names unquenchable fire. The images concern different forms of rejected growth and do not identify Isaiah's historical scene with the baptismal address.
source_text: Their strength will become a stalk of tow and their works sparks of fire. The lawless and sinners will be burned together, with no one to quench.”

target_units.text: Already the axe lies at the root of the trees. Every tree, therefore, that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire.
I baptize you in water for repentance, but the One coming after me is stronger than I, whose sandals I am not fit to carry. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.
His winnowing shovel is in His hand, and He will thoroughly clear His threshing floor and gather His wheat into the storehouse; but He will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

relationship: named counterpart to Isaiah's prophetic record
rationale: Isaiah's heading names the Lord's revelation to Isaiah son of Amos concerning Judea and Jerusalem; Chronicles likewise attributes prophecy to Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Hezekiah's deeds. The shared named prophet is specific, while Chronicles does not identify this particular oracle.
source_text: The word that came from the Lord to Isaiah son of Amos concerning Judea and Jerusalem.

target_units.text: The rest of Hezekiah’s deeds and his mercy are written in the prophecy of Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet and in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.

relationship: close parallel of the exalted mountain attracting peoples
rationale: Both place the Lord's mountain on mountain summits and above the hills in the last days and describe peoples coming toward it. Isaiah explicitly includes God's house and all nations.
source_text: In the last days the Lord’s mountain and God’s house will be clearly visible on the summits of the mountains and be raised above the hills; all the nations will come to it,

target_units.text: In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, established upon the mountain summits and raised above the hills, and peoples will hurry toward it.

relationship: close parallel of nations seeking Zion's instruction
rationale: Both give the nations' invitation to ascend the Lord's mountain and Jacob's God's house, learn His way and walk in it; both conclude that law goes from Zion and the Lord's word from Jerusalem.
source_text: and many nations will go and say, “Come, let us go up to the Lord’s mountain and to the house of Jacob’s God. He will announce His way to us, and we will walk in it.” For law will go out from Zion, and the Lord’s word from Jerusalem.

target_units.text: Many nations will go and say, “Come, let us go up to the Lord’s mountain and to the house of Jacob’s God. They will show us His way, and we will walk in His paths.” For law will go out from Zion, and the Lord’s word from Jerusalem.

relationship: close parallel of judgment and weapons remade for farming
rationale: Both join divine judgment among peoples with swords made into plows, spears into sickles and the cessation of nations learning war. Micah adds strong nations reaching a distant land.
source_text: He will judge between the nations and reprove a numerous people. They will beat their swords into plows and their spears into sickles. Nation will no longer take sword against nation, and they will certainly no longer learn to wage war.

target_units.text: He will judge between many peoples and reprove strong nations as far as a distant land. They will cut their swords into plows and their spears into sickles. Nation will certainly no longer raise sword against nation, nor will they learn to wage war anymore.

relationship: related exhortation to walk in the Lord's light
rationale: Isaiah invites Jacob's house to walk by the Lord's light; Ephesians likewise describes people as light in the Lord and commands walking as children of light, explaining its fruit as goodness, righteousness and truth.
source_text: And now, house of Jacob, come, let us walk by the Lord’s light!

target_units.text: For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light,
for the fruit of the light is in all goodness and righteousness and truth,
testing what is pleasing to the Lord.

relationship: law background for foreign omen practices
rationale: Isaiah indicts the country for omens like foreign peoples' practices; Deuteronomy forbids learning the nations' divination and omens. The separate reference to foreign children is not explained by this law.
source_text: For He abandoned His people, Israel’s house, because their country was filled, as from the beginning, with omens like the foreigners’ country, and many foreign children were born to them.

target_units.text: And when you enter the land which the Lord your God gives you, you shall not learn to do after the abominations of those nations.
There shall not be found among you one who purifies his son or his daughter by fire, or practises divination, or interprets spoken omens, or observes auguries, or works sorcery,
or chants spells, or is a medium, or observes portents, or inquires of the dead.
For everyone who does these things is an abomination unto the Lord your God; for because of these abominations the Lord shall destroy them from before you.
You shall be perfect before the Lord your God.
For these nations whose possession you inherit hearken unto omens and divinations; but the Lord your God has not granted you so to do.

relationship: related warning about multiplying horses and precious wealth
rationale: Isaiah describes a country full of horses, silver and gold; Deuteronomy forbids the ruler to multiply horses and greatly multiply silver and gold. The law addresses the ruler specifically, whereas Isaiah describes the land.
source_text: For their country was filled with silver and gold, and their treasures had no number; the land was filled with horses, and their chariots had no number.

target_units.text: For he shall not multiply horses unto himself, neither shall he cause the people to return unto Egypt, that he may multiply horses unto himself; for the Lord has said: You shall not return by this way again.
And he shall not multiply wives unto himself, neither shall his heart turn aside; and he shall not greatly multiply silver and gold unto himself.

relationship: close worship of handmade idols
rationale: Isaiah indicts people for bowing to what their hands and fingers made; the psalm likewise calls the nations' idols works of human hands and addresses their makers and those trusting them.
source_text: The land was filled with abominations, the works of their hands, and they bowed before what their fingers made.

target_units.text: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, works of human hands.
They have a mouth and will not speak; they have eyes and will not see.
They have ears and will not hear; they have noses and will not smell.
They have hands and will not feel; feet, and will not walk; they will not sound with their throat.
May those who make them become like them, and all who have put their trust in them.

relationship: related humiliation of those bowing to idols
rationale: Within Isaiah's indictment of handmade worship, the human bows and is humbled without release; the psalm likewise calls those bowing to carved images to shame. The forms of humiliation are expressed differently.
source_text: A human being bowed down, and a man was humbled; I will certainly not let them go.

target_units.text: Let all who bow down to carved images be ashamed, those who boast in their idols. Bow down to Him, all His angels!

relationship: parallel attempts to hide from divine judgment
rationale: Isaiah commands entering rocks and hiding in earth before the Lord's terror; Amos likewise depicts people burrowing below or hiding on Carmel as God searches them out. Amos explicitly denies successful escape, which Isaiah's individual sentence does not state.
source_text: And now enter the rocks and hide in the earth from the Lord’s terror and the glory of His strength, whenever He rises to shatter the earth.

target_units.text: If they burrow into Hades, My hand will pull them up from there; if they climb to heaven, I will bring them down from there.
If they hide on Carmel’s summit, I will search them out and take them from there. If they plunge from My eyes into the sea’s depths, I will command the dragon there, and it will bite them.

relationship: related divine humbling of human height
rationale: Isaiah contrasts the Lord's high eyes with humanity brought low; the psalm likewise attributes humbling the arrogant's eyes to God. The high eyes in Isaiah belong to the Lord, not to the arrogant people described in the psalm.
source_text: For the Lord’s eyes are high, but the human being is low; humanity’s height will be humbled, and the Lord alone will be exalted on that day.

target_units.text: For Thou wilt save a lowly people and humble the eyes of the arrogant.

relationship: parallel downfall of insolence
rationale: Isaiah announces the Lord's day against insolent and elevated people who will be humbled; Proverbs likewise places insolence before ruin and evil-mindedness before a fall. It does not name the prophetic day.
source_text: For the Lord Sabaoth has a day against every insolent and arrogant person, against everyone high and elevated; they will be humbled,

target_units.text: Insolence leads before ruin, and evil-mindedness before a fall.

relationship: close judgment imagery of Lebanon's cedars and Bashan's oaks
rationale: Both place Lebanon's cedars and Bashan's oaks under devastation. Isaiah lists them among the high things facing the Lord's day; Zechariah commands lament because the mighty forest has fallen.
source_text: against every cedar of Lebanon among the high and elevated, and against every oak tree of Bashan,

target_units.text: Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars!
Let the pine wail, for the cedar has fallen, because the mighty have suffered greatly! Wail, Bashan’s oaks, for the thick-grown forest has been torn down!

relationship: close mountains and heights affected by divine arrival
rationale: Isaiah includes every mountain and high hill in the Lord's judgment; Micah likewise describes the Lord descending upon earth's heights and mountains shaking beneath Him.
source_text: against every mountain and every high hill,

target_units.text: For look, the Lord is coming out of His place; He will descend and step upon the heights of the earth,
and the mountains will be shaken beneath Him, and the valleys will melt like wax before fire and like water flowing downhill.

relationship: parallel divine judgment against walls and towers

rationale: Both describe people casting away or removing silver-and-gold idols. Isaiah 2 names worthless ones and bats as the destination; Isaiah 30 instead describes smashing and pushing the idols away through defilement images.

rationale: Isaiah describes entering rock holes and clefts in terror; Jesus warns Jerusalem's daughters of days when people ask mountains to fall and hills to cover them. Seeking a cleft and asking the heights to cover are distinct expressions of desperation.

relationship: close removal of Jerusalem's bread and water support
rationale: Isaiah says the Lord will remove the strength of bread and water; Ezekiel likewise says God breaks Jerusalem's support of bread and reduces bread and water to scarcity.

rationale: Isaiah includes warriors, judges, prophets and elders among the supports removed; Kings describes Jerusalem losing rulers and mighty fighting men through deportation. It supports the loss of leadership and military strength without supplying every office in Isaiah's list.

relationship: close warning about a young ruler
rationale: Isaiah describes young men installed as rulers amid judgment; Ecclesiastes likewise pronounces woe on a city whose king is young. Isaiah's mockers and Ecclesiastes's morning feasting are their separate details.

rationale: Isaiah describes children colliding with elders and people against neighbors; Micah likewise depicts sons dishonoring fathers and hostility within households. Each depicts broken social relations through its own specified pairs.

relationship: related rebellious speech and divine opposition
rationale: Isaiah links Jerusalem's fall with tongues accompanying lawlessness and disobedience; the psalm likewise seeks the destruction of boastful tongues that claim their lips are their own and ask who is their lord.

target_units.text: May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and a boastful tongue—

relationship: narrative background for brazen sin like Sodom's
rationale: Isaiah says the people publicly announce their sin like Sodom; Genesis depicts Sodom's crowd openly demanding access to the guests and threatening Lot. The narrative illustrates public lawlessness without asserting that every act in Isaiah is the same offense.

relationship: close plot against a troublesome righteous person
rationale: Isaiah reports the proposal to bind the righteous because he is troublesome; Wisdom's ungodly speakers likewise propose lying in wait for the righteous because he is troublesome and opposes their works.
