When your eyes see another woman, then your mouth will speak crooked things,
and you will lie down as in the heart of the sea, and like a helmsman in heavy surging;
and you will say, “They strike me, and I felt no pain; they mocked me, but I did not know. When will dawn come, so that I may go and seek those with whom I will gather?”

relationship: parallel music and wine amid culpable indifference
rationale: Isaiah's musical wine feast disregards the Lord's works; Amos describes luxurious eating, instruments, and wine without suffering over Joseph's shattering. Both connect festive indulgence with neglected obligations, while the neglected object differs.
source_text: For with lyre and harp, drums and flutes they drink wine, but they do not look at the Lord’s works or consider the works of His hands.

target_units.text: sleeping upon ivory beds and indulging upon your couches, eating young goats from the flocks and milk-fed calves from the herds,
clapping to the sound of instruments; they reckoned them as lasting, not passing away,
drinking strained wine and anointing yourselves with the finest perfumes, yet suffering nothing over Joseph’s shattering.

relationship: parallel judgment associated with failure to know God
rationale: Isaiah explains captivity and deadly deprivation by the people's not knowing the Lord; Hosea connects the people's lack of knowledge and rejection of recognition with divine rejection. Hosea does not repeat Isaiah's particular famine and captivity details.
source_text: Therefore My people became captive because they did not know the Lord, and there was a multitude of dead through famine and thirst for water.

target_units.text: My people were likened to one without knowledge. Because you thrust away recognition, I too will thrust you away from serving Me as priest. You forgot your God’s law, and I too will forget your children.

relationship: shared image of Hades' enlarged appetite
rationale: Isaiah portrays Hades opening an unceasing mouth to receive the city's great and rich; Habakkuk compares a boastful man's widened, unsatisfied appetite to Hades and death. The image corresponds, while Isaiah describes Hades itself and Habakkuk a human resemblance.
source_text: Hades enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth without ceasing, and her glorious ones, great ones, rich ones and pestilent ones will go down.

target_units.text: But the wine-soaked, contemptuous, boastful man will accomplish nothing. He widened his appetite like Hades and is like death, never filled; he will gather all nations and receive all peoples to himself.

relationship: parallel humbling of lofty eyes
rationale: Isaiah announces the dishonoring of human beings and humbling of lofty eyes; the psalm addresses God as the One who humbles arrogant eyes while saving a humble people.
source_text: A human being will be humbled, a man dishonored, and lofty eyes humbled.

target_units.text: For Thou wilt save a lowly people and humble the eyes of the arrogant.

relationship: parallel divine glory displayed through judgment
rationale: Isaiah says the holy God will be exalted through judgment and glorified through righteousness; Ezekiel says the Lord will be glorified and sanctified in Sidon when He executes judgments there. The settings differ, but both explicitly join judgment and God's manifested honor.
source_text: The Lord Sabaoth will be exalted through judgment, and the holy God will be glorified through righteousness.

target_units.text: and say: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am against you, Sidon, and I will be glorified in you. You will know that I am the Lord when I execute judgments in you, and I will be sanctified in you.

relationship: related pasture imagery after the land's upheaval
rationale: Isaiah 5 portrays plundered people pastured like bulls and lambs feeding in deserted places; Isaiah 7 describes land becoming sheep pasture and cattle trampling ground. Both use cattle and sheep in transformed land, without equating the figurative people of 5:17 with the animals of 7:25.
source_text: Those who were plundered will be pastured like bulls, and lambs will feed upon the deserted places of those wiped out.

target_units.text: Every mountain that is plowed will be plowed, and fear will certainly not come there; for from fallow ground and thorn it will become pasture for sheep and a trampling place for cattle.

relationship: shared cords-of-sin imagery with differing agency
rationale: Isaiah condemns people drawing sins with a long cord; Proverbs depicts people bound tightly by the cords of their own sins. The same binding image exposes attachment to wrongdoing, but Isaiah emphasizes drawing sins and Proverbs being caught by them.
source_text: Woe to those drawing sins as with a long cord and lawless deeds as with the strap of a heifer’s yoke,

target_units.text: Lawless acts hunt a man, and each is bound tight by the cords of his own sins.

relationship: parallel taunt demanding arrival of the Lord's word
rationale: Isaiah quotes those insisting that God's work and counsel come quickly so they may see; Jeremiah reports opponents asking where the Lord's word is and demanding that it come. Both challenge prophetic warning by demanding its realization.
source_text: who say, “Let what He will do approach quickly, so that we may see, and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel come, so that we may know!”

target_units.text: Behold, they say to me: Where is the Lord’s word? Let it come!

relationship: particular judicial instance of reversing good and evil
rationale: Isaiah condemns calling evil good and good evil; Proverbs calls judging the unjust righteous and the righteous unjust detestable before God. The target supplies a concrete moral-verdict reversal, rather than repeating Isaiah's light and flavor images.
source_text: Woe to those calling evil good and good evil, making darkness light and light darkness, making bitter sweet and sweet bitter!

target_units.text: One who judges the unjust righteous and the righteous unjust is unclean and detestable before God.

relationship: parallel rejection of self-estimated wisdom
rationale: Isaiah pronounces woe on those discerning in their own judgment and knowledgeable in their own view; Proverbs commands a person not to be prudent in one's own estimation, but to fear God and turn from evil.
source_text: Woe to those who are discerning in their own judgment and knowledgeable in their own view!

target_units.text: Do not be prudent in your own estimation; fear God and turn away from every evil.

relationship: parallel warning about powerful drinkers
rationale: Isaiah condemns strong and powerful people drinking and mixing intoxicants; Proverbs warns the powerful against wine lest they forget wisdom and become unable to judge the weak rightly. Isaiah's following verse similarly exposes corrupted judgment.
source_text: Woe to your strong ones who drink wine and the powerful who mix strong drink,

target_units.text: Do everything with counsel; drink wine with counsel. The powerful are hot-tempered, but let them not drink wine,
so that, after drinking, they may not forget wisdom and become entirely unable to judge the weak rightly.

relationship: parallel condemnation of bribed judgments
rationale: Isaiah describes gifts used to justify the ungodly and remove the righteous person's right; Deuteronomy prohibits bribes because they blind the wise and overthrow the words of the righteous.
source_text: who justify the ungodly for gifts and take away the righteous person’s right!

target_units.text: They shall not pervert judgment, neither shall they show partiality, nor take a bribe; for bribes blind the eyes of the wise, and overthrow the words of the righteous.

relationship: parallel fire judgment expressed through root and plant destruction
rationale: Isaiah compares the condemned to a stalk burned by fire, with root like chaff and blossom like dust; Malachi depicts practitioners of lawlessness as straw burned until neither root nor branch remains. Both join fiery plant imagery to judgment on wrongdoing.
source_text: Therefore, as a stalk is burned by a fiery coal and consumed by a rising flame, their root will become like chaff and their blossom rise like dust. For they did not desire the law of the Lord Sabaoth, but provoked the utterance of the Holy One of Israel.

target_units.text: For look, the day of the Lord is coming, burning like an oven, and it will burn them. All the foreigners and all who practice lawlessness will be straw, and the coming day will ignite them,” says the Lord Almighty, “and neither root nor branch will remain from them.

relationship: repeated refrain of unspent anger and the high hand
rationale: Both passages conclude that despite the announced blows the anger has not turned away and the hand is still high. This is a distinctive repeated judgment refrain, while the surrounding descriptions of the blows differ.
source_text: The Lord Sabaoth was enraged with wrath against His people, brought His hand against them and struck them. The mountains were roused, and their carcasses became like dung in the middle of the road. In all these things the anger did not turn away, but the hand is still high.

target_units.text: Syria from the sun’s rising and the Greeks from the sun’s setting, who devour Israel with their whole mouth. For all these things the anger did not turn away, but the hand is still high.

relationship: parallel summoning of a swift distant nation
rationale: Isaiah describes God signaling nations from the earth's end, who arrive quickly; Deuteronomy warns that the Lord will bring a nation from afar and the earth's end with eagle-like speed. The target also characterizes that invader's ruthlessness.
source_text: Therefore He will raise a signal among the distant nations and whistle to them from the earth’s end. Behold, they come quickly and lightly!

target_units.text: The Lord shall bring against you a nation from afar, from the end of the earth, as the swooping of an eagle, a nation whose speech you shall not understand,
a nation shameless of countenance, which shall not regard the face of the aged, nor have mercy upon the young.

relationship: parallel comparison of attacking chariots to a storm
rationale: Isaiah likens the invaders' chariot wheels to a storm; Jeremiah likens the approaching enemy's chariots to a storm and adds eagle-swift horses. The shared martial-weather image does not supply Isaiah's rock-like hoof detail.
source_text: Their arrows are sharp and their bows drawn. Their horses’ feet were reckoned like solid rock, and their chariot wheels like a storm.

target_units.text: Behold, he will come up like a cloud, and his chariots like a storm; his horses are swifter than eagles. Woe to us, because we suffer misery!

relationship: parallel lion-like seizure without rescue
rationale: Isaiah's attacking force rushes like lions and seizes without anyone rescuing; Hosea portrays the Lord Himself as a lion to Judah, seizing and taking with no rescuer. The image and helplessness correspond, while the immediate agents differ.
source_text: They rush like lions and have taken their stand like a lion’s cub. It will seize and cry out as a beast does and cast out, and no one will rescue them.

target_units.text: For I am like a panther to Ephraim and like a lion to Judah’s house. I seize and will go away and take, and there will be no one to rescue.

relationship: parallel darkness as the character of judgment
rationale: Isaiah's threatened people look toward the earth and find harsh darkness and perplexity; Amos warns that the Lord's day is darkness rather than light. Both use darkness to describe the experience of judgment.
source_text: It will cry out because of them on that day like the sound of a surging sea. They will look to the earth, and behold, harsh darkness in their perplexity.

target_units.text: Woe to those desiring the Lord’s day! Why is this Lord’s day for you? It is darkness, not light,
as when someone flees from a lion and a bear falls upon him, then leaps into his house, braces his hands upon the wall, and a snake bites him.
Is not the Lord’s day darkness rather than light, gloom that has no brightness in it?

relationship: parallel cry compared with a surging sea
rationale: Isaiah 5 compares the cry to a surging sea; Isaiah 17 explicitly compares many nations' roaring and disturbance to a surging sea and rushing water. This counterpart concerns sound within accounts of invasion.
source_text: It will cry out because of them on that day like the sound of a surging sea. They will look to the earth, and behold, harsh darkness in their perplexity.

target_units.text: Woe, the multitude of many nations! Like a surging sea, so you will be troubled, and the back of many nations will roar like water.

Many nations are like abundant water, like much water violently rushing down. He will drive him away and pursue him far off, like chaff-dust when people winnow before wind, and like wheel-dust carried by a squall.

relationship: parallel prophetic vision of the enthroned Lord
rationale: Isaiah sees the Lord on a high throne with the house full of His glory; Micaiah sees the Lord on His throne surrounded by heaven's army. Both introduce a heavenly scene preceding a commission, without identifying their different attendants.
source_text: In the year that King Oziah died, I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and lifted up; and the house was full of His glory.

target_units.text: Micaiah said, “Not so—not I! Hear the Lord’s word—not so! I saw the Lord, the God of Israel, sitting on His throne, and all the army of heaven stood around Him, on His right and His left.

relationship: New Testament identification of Isaiah's vision of glory
rationale: After citing Isaiah's words about blinded eyes and a hardened heart, John says Isaiah saw His glory and spoke concerning Him. In John's discussion of unbelief toward Jesus, this explicitly connects Isaiah's glory vision with Jesus.
source_text: In the year that King Oziah died, I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and lifted up; and the house was full of His glory.

target_units.text: For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said again,
“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with the eyes and understand with the heart and turn—and I will heal them.”
Isaiah said these things because he saw His glory and spoke concerning Him.

relationship: related throne-vision creatures using wings to cover themselves
rationale: Isaiah's seraphim have six wings, with pairs covering faces and feet and enabling flight; Ezekiel's living creatures have four wings, two of which cover their bodies. The comparison concerns winged attendants and covering, while preserving their different kinds, numbers, and arrangements.
source_text: And seraphim stood around Him: each one had six wings, and each one had six wings; with two they covered their faces, and with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew.

target_units.text: and each had four faces, and each had four wings.
Their legs were straight, and their feet were winged, with sparks like flashing bronze; and their wings were light.
A human hand was beneath their wings on their four sides; and the faces of all four of them
did not turn as they walked; each went straight ahead.
The likeness of their faces was a human face and a lion’s face on the right for all four, and a calf’s face on the left for all four, and an eagle’s face for all four.
The wings of all four were stretched out above; each had two joined to one another, and two covered the top of their bodies.

relationship: parallel declaration of the Lord's glory throughout the earth
rationale: The seraphim proclaim that all the earth is full of the Lord's glory; in Numbers the Lord declares that His glory shall fill all the earth. The universal glory claim corresponds, while Isaiah adds the threefold acclamation of holiness.
source_text: And one cried to another, saying: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord Sabaoth; all the earth is full of His glory.

target_units.text: But as I live, and as My name lives, the glory of the Lord shall fill all the earth;

relationship: related smoke and powerful sound at divine manifestation
rationale: Isaiah's house fills with smoke at the attendants' cry; Sinai is covered with smoke at God's fiery descent, accompanied by strong trumpet sounds. Both associate the divine manifestation with smoke and overwhelming sound; Exodus here does not state that Isaiah's lintel event recurs.
source_text: And the lintel was lifted at the sound of their cry, and the house was filled with smoke.

target_units.text: Toward dawn on the third day there were thunder and lightning and a dark cloud over Mount Sinai. The trumpet sounded loudly, and all the people in the camp were terrified.
Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stood beneath the mountain.
Mount Sinai was entirely covered with smoke because God had descended on it in fire. The smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace, and all the people were greatly astonished.
The trumpet’s sounds grew much stronger. Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice.

relationship: parallel confession of unworthiness before a manifestation of the Lord
rationale: Isaiah confesses unclean lips and a pierced heart after seeing the King; Peter confesses that he is a sinful man after Jesus' extraordinary catch of fish. Both confessions precede a mission, with different encounters and forms of sin-consciousness.
source_text: And I said, Woe is me, for I am pierced to the heart! For I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips; and my eyes have seen the King, the Lord Sabaoth.

target_units.text: When Simon Peter saw it, he fell at Jesus’ knees, saying, “Depart from me, Lord, because I am a sinful man.”
For amazement had seized him and everyone with him at the catch of fish they had taken,
and likewise James and John, Zebedee’s sons, who were Simon’s partners. Jesus said to Simon, “Do not fear. From now on you will be catching people alive.”

relationship: related altar coals brought into the divine presence
rationale: Isaiah's seraph takes a coal from the altar for the encounter with the prophet; Aaron brings burning altar coals within the veil and uses incense before the Lord. The altar-coal setting corresponds, but the priestly incense rite is not the same action as Isaiah's cleansing.
source_text: And one of the seraphim was sent to me, with a coal in his hand that he had taken from the altar with the tongs;

target_units.text: And he shall take the firepan full of burning coals from the altar opposite the Lord, fill his hands with finely compounded incense, and bring them within the veil,
and put the incense on the fire before the Lord. The vapour of incense shall cover the propitiatory cover above the testimonies, and he shall not die.

relationship: parallel touching of a prophet's mouth before commission
rationale: Isaiah's lips are touched with the coal to remove iniquity and cleanse sins; the Lord touches Jeremiah's mouth to put His words there. Both prepare a prophet's speech through a touch, while the explicitly stated effects differ.
source_text: and he touched my mouth and said, Behold, this has touched your lips, and will take away your iniquities and cleanse your sins.

target_units.text: The Lord stretched out His hand toward me and touched my mouth. The Lord said to me, Behold, I have put My words into your mouth.

relationship: parallel heavenly question followed by a volunteer
rationale: The Lord asks whom to send and Isaiah volunteers; in Micaiah's vision the Lord asks who will deceive Ahab and a spirit volunteers. The council question-and-response pattern corresponds; Isaiah's prophetic mission is not equated with the spirit's deceptive mission.
source_text: And I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And I said, Behold, here I am; send me.

target_units.text: The Lord said, ‘Who will deceive Ahab king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Remmath-gilead?’ One said this, and another said that.
A spirit came forward, stood before the Lord, and said, ‘I will deceive him.’ The Lord said to it, ‘By what means?’
It said, ‘I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ He said, ‘You will deceive him and indeed prevail. Go out and do so.’

relationship: explicit quotation of Isaiah's uncomprehending hearing and sight
rationale: Matthew names Isaiah's prophecy and quotes the repeated hearing without understanding and seeing without perception, applying it to the hearers of Jesus' parables.
source_text: And He said, Go, and say to this people: Hearing, you will hear and certainly not understand; and seeing, you will see and certainly not perceive.

target_units.text: In them is fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy, which says: ‘You will hear and hear but certainly not understand; you will look and look but certainly not see.

For the heart of this people has grown fat, and with their ears they heard with difficulty, and they closed their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn, and I will heal them.’

relationship: explicit quotation of Isaiah's unresponsive people
rationale: Paul attributes the words to the Holy Spirit through Isaiah and repeats the dull heart, heavy ears, closed eyes, and the clause about turning and healing. Acts applies the quotation amid divided responses to Paul's witness about Jesus.
source_text: For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I will heal them.

target_units.text: Disagreeing with one another, they began to leave after Paul made one statement: “The Holy Spirit spoke well through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers,
saying, ‘Go to this people and say: “You will hear and hear, yet never understand; you will look and look, yet never see.

For this people’s heart has grown dull, their ears have become hard of hearing, and they have closed their eyes, lest they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn back, and I would heal them.”’

relationship: related quotation with a different statement of agency
rationale: John uses Isaiah's eye-and-heart language to explain unbelief toward Jesus, stating that He blinded their eyes and hardened their heart. Isaiah's supplied wording says the people closed their eyes; the connection preserves this difference rather than substituting one form for the other.
source_text: For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I will heal them.

target_units.text: For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said again,
“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with the eyes and understand with the heart and turn—and I will heal them.”
Isaiah said these things because he saw His glory and spoke concerning Him.

relationship: parallel depopulation of cities under divine judgment
rationale: Isaiah's answer to how long describes empty cities, houses without people, and a desolate land; Jeremiah depicts no human present, ruined cities, and every city abandoned in the Lord's announced judgment.
source_text: And I said, How long, O Lord? And He said: Until cities lie waste, without inhabitants, and houses, without people, and the land is left desolate.

target_units.text: I looked, and behold, there was no human, and all the birds of heaven were terrified.
I saw, and behold, Carmel was a wilderness, and all the cities were burned with fire before the Lord, and they vanished before His furious anger.
Thus says the Lord: The whole land will be a wilderness, but I will certainly not make a complete end.
For these things let the earth mourn and let heaven above grow dark, because I have spoken and will not change My mind; I have set Myself in motion and will not turn back from it.
At the sound of a horseman and a drawn bow the whole countryside withdrew; they entered caves and hid in groves and climbed onto the rocks. Every city was abandoned; no human dwells in them.

relationship: parallel removal of the people far from their land
rationale: Isaiah says God will remove people far away; Deuteronomy warns of removal from the land and scattering among nations from end to end of the earth. This supports the removal clause; it does not supply Isaiah's following statement that those remaining will multiply.
source_text: And after these things God will remove people far away; and those who remain will multiply upon the land.

target_units.text: And it shall be, as the Lord rejoiced over you to do you good and to multiply you, so shall the Lord rejoice over you to destroy you; and you shall be removed from the land whither you go to inherit it.

And the Lord your God shall scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth unto the other; and there you shall serve other gods, wood and stone, which neither you nor your fathers have known.

relationship: related tenth remaining after judgment
rationale: Isaiah speaks of a tenth remaining, then exposed again to plunder; Amos describes a hundred remaining from a thousand and ten from a hundred. The shared remnant fraction is specific, while Amos does not repeat Isaiah's further plunder or tree imagery.
source_text: And yet a tenth remains upon it; and again it will be for plunder, as a terebinth, and as an acorn when it falls from its husk.

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord, the Lord: “From the city out of which a thousand went, a hundred will remain, and from the one out of which a hundred went, ten will remain for Israel’s house.”

relationship: parallel account of the Aramean and Israelite attack under Achaz
rationale: Both name Raasson and Phakee coming against Jerusalem in the reign of Achaz/Ahaz. The supplied accounts differ in describing the siege: Isaiah says they could not besiege her, while Kings says they besieged Ahaz but could not wage the battle successfully.
source_text: In the days of Achaz, son of Joatham, son of Oziah, king of Judea, Raasson king of Aram and Phakee son of Romelias, king of Israel, went up against Jerusalem to wage war on her, but they could not besiege her.

target_units.text: Then Raasson king of Syria and Phakee son of Romelias, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem for war. They besieged Ahaz but could not wage the battle successfully.

relationship: historical counterpart to the threat from Aram and Ephraim
rationale: Isaiah reports alarm at Aram's agreement with Ephraim; Chronicles describes Ahaz delivered into the hands of Syria's king and Israel's king, followed by major losses. This supports the two-front pressure in his reign without claiming that Chronicles repeats the agreement or tree simile.
source_text: It was reported to David’s house, “Aram has come to agreement with Ephraim.” His soul and his people’s soul were distraught, as when a tree in a wood is shaken by wind.

target_units.text: The Lord his God delivered him through the hand of Syria’s king, who struck him, took a great number of captives from them, and brought them to Damascus. He also delivered him into Israel’s king’s hands, and the king struck him a great blow.
Phakee son of Romelia, king of Israel, killed one hundred twenty thousand men mighty in strength in Judah in one day, because they had abandoned the Lord, the God of their fathers.
Ezekri, the mighty man of Ephraim, killed Maasaias the king’s son, Esdrikam the ruler of his house, and Elkana, the king’s deputy.
The sons of Israel took captive three hundred thousand of their brethren: women, sons, and daughters. They took many spoils from them and brought the spoils to Samaria.

relationship: related pool and fuller's-field setting in a later crisis
rationale: Isaiah is sent to Achaz toward the pool of the upper road of the fuller's field; the Assyrian envoys later stand at the upper pool's aqueduct on the road of the Fuller's Field under Hezekiah. Both join a pool, road, and fuller's field, with different kings and visitors and differently phrased location descriptions.
source_text: The Lord said to Isaiah, “Go out to meet Achaz, you and the remaining Jasub, your son, toward the pool of the upper road of the fuller’s field,

target_units.text: The king of the Assyrians sent Tharthan, Raphis, and Rhapsakes from Lachish to King Hezekiah against Jerusalem with a great force. They went up, came to Jerusalem, and stood at the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road of the Fuller’s Field.

relationship: parallel summons to courage and quiet before military danger
rationale: Isaiah tells the threatened king to be quiet and not fear; Moses tells frightened Israel to take courage and keep silence as the Lord fights for them. The shared response to military danger does not identify the two crises.
source_text: and you will say to him, ‘Take care to be quiet, and do not fear; do not let your soul grow weak before these two smoking firebrand logs. For whenever the wrath of My anger comes, I will heal again.

target_units.text: And Moses said to the people, “Take courage; stand, and behold the salvation from God, which He shall accomplish for us today. For as you have seen the Egyptians today, you shall see them no more for ever.
The Lord shall fight for you, and you shall keep silence.”

relationship: related hostile rulers' plotting
rationale: Isaiah introduces the hostile counsel of the Aramean and Israelite rulers; the psalm depicts rulers gathering and devising opposition to the Lord and His anointed. Both expose hostile political counsel, without identifying Achaz with the psalm's anointed figure.
source_text: And the son of Aram and the son of Romelias, because they counseled an evil counsel concerning you, saying,

target_units.text: Why did nations rage, and peoples meditate on empty things?
The kings of the earth stood ready, and the rulers gathered together, against the Lord and against His anointed. Diapsalma.
“Let us tear apart their bonds and cast their yoke away from us.”

relationship: contrasting attempts at foreign installation of a Judean king
rationale: Isaiah reports a plan to install Tabeel's son, which the next verse declares will fail; Kings records Pharaoh Nechao actually installing Eliakim in Judah. Both concern foreign control of Judah's succession, but involve different candidates and opposite outcomes.
source_text: “We will go up into Judea and, after speaking with them, turn them toward ourselves and make Tabeel’s son king over her,”

target_units.text: Pharaoh Nechao made Eliakim, son of Josiah king of Judah, king over them in place of his father Josiah and changed his name to Joakim. He took Joachas and brought him into Egypt, and he died there.

relationship: parallel frustration of human political counsel by God
rationale: The Lord declares that the coalition's counsel will not endure or occur; the psalm says He scatters nations' counsels and nullifies rulers' plans, whereas His own counsel remains.
source_text: thus says the Lord Sabaoth: “This counsel will certainly not endure, nor will it happen.

target_units.text: The Lord scatters the counsels of nations; He nullifies the plans of peoples and nullifies the counsels of rulers.
But the Lord’s counsel remains for ever, the plans of His heart from generation to generation.

relationship: later historical counterpart to Ephraim's political collapse
rationale: Isaiah announces that Ephraim's kingdom will cease from being a people; Kings recounts Assyria's capture of Samaria and deportation of Israel. The historical loss of kingdom and population corresponds, without claiming that this target establishes the stated sixty-five-year interval.
source_text: But the head of Aram is Damascus; yet within another sixty-five years Ephraim’s kingdom will cease from being a people,

target_units.text: The king of the Assyrians went up through the whole land, went up to Samaria, and besieged it for three years.
In Hoshea’s ninth year the king of the Assyrians captured Samaria and deported Israel to the Assyrians. He settled them in Alae and Abor, rivers of Gozan, and Ore of the Medes.

relationship: parallel dependence of understanding upon faith
rationale: Isaiah says that without believing the hearers will not understand; Hebrews says that by faith we understand the ages to have been formed by God's word. Both connect faith and understanding, though their objects are political warning and creation respectively.
source_text: and the head of Ephraim is Somoron, and the head of Somoron Romelias’s son. If you do not believe, you will certainly not understand.”’”

target_units.text: By faith we understand that the ages were formed by God’s word, so that what is seen did not come into being from visible things.

relationship: related invitation and request for a confirming sign
rationale: Achaz is invited to ask for a sign from the Lord; Hezekiah later asks Isaiah for a sign of the Lord's promise and receives the returning shadow. The shared royal encounter with Isaiah and a divine sign contrasts with Achaz's following refusal.
source_text: Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth or in the height.

target_units.text: Hezekiah said to Isaiah, ‘What is the sign that the Lord will heal me and I shall go up to the Lord’s house on the third day?’
Isaiah said, ‘This is the sign from the Lord that the Lord will do the word He has spoken: The shadow will advance ten steps, if it returns ten steps.’
Hezekiah said, ‘It is easy for the shadow to incline ten steps. No, let the shadow return ten steps backward.’
Isaiah the prophet cried to the Lord, and the shadow returned backward ten steps on the stairway.

relationship: verbal appeal to the prohibition on testing the Lord
rationale: Achaz says he will not put the Lord to the test, matching the law's prohibition on testing Him. Isaiah's following rebuke prevents treating this verbal resemblance as approval of Achaz's refusal of an expressly offered sign.
source_text: And Achaz said, I will certainly not ask, nor will I put the Lord to the test at all.

target_units.text: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test, as you tested Him at Testing.

relationship: related human opposition reaching the Lord Himself
rationale: Isaiah asks why David's house troubles the Lord as well as people; Moses says the congregation's murmuring against the human leaders is against God. Both expose a divine dimension in opposition directed through God's representatives, in different historical settings.
source_text: And he said, Hear now, O house of David: is it a small thing for you to trouble people? And how is it that you trouble the Lord?

target_units.text: and in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord, when He hears your murmuring against God. And what are we, that you murmur against us?”

And Moses said, “When the Lord gives you meat to eat in the evening, and bread in the morning until you are full, it is because the Lord has heard your murmuring with which you murmur against us. And what are we? For your murmuring is not against us, but against God.”

relationship: explicit virgin-and-Emmanuel quotation applied to Jesus' birth
rationale: Matthew introduces the virgin conceiving and bearing a son named Emmanuel as a prophetic fulfillment in the birth of Jesus, reproducing Isaiah's distinctive sign and name.
source_text: Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: behold, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel.

target_units.text: All this has happened so that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled:
“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call His name Emmanuel”; which means “God with us.”

relationship: same-chapter recurrence of the child's diet in the remnant's food
rationale: The child eats curds and honey; later in the same chapter the remaining people eat butter and honey because of abundant milk. The repeated dairy-and-honey diet links the child sign with the chapter's description of life in the land.
source_text: Curds and honey he will eat; before he knows or chooses evil, he will choose the good.

target_units.text: On that day a person will raise a heifer from the cattle and two sheep,
and because they produce very much milk, everyone left upon the land will eat butter and honey.

relationship: parallel description of children before knowledge of good and evil
rationale: Isaiah places the sign before the child knows good or evil, while describing his refusal of wickedness; Deuteronomy describes young children who do not yet know good or evil and will inherit the land. The developmental description corresponds without equating the separate land promises.
source_text: For before the child knows good or evil, he refuses wickedness, to choose the good; and the land which you fear because of the two kings will be forsaken.

target_units.text: And every young child who this day knows neither good nor evil shall enter there; and I will give it unto them, and they shall inherit it.

relationship: historical counterpart concerning the removal of one feared king
rationale: Isaiah announces the forsaking of the land feared because of two kings; Kings records Assyria capturing Damascus and killing Raasson, one of those kings. The target supports that particular ruler's removal, not both kings or the child's age chronology.
source_text: For before the child knows good or evil, he refuses wickedness, to choose the good; and the land which you fear because of the two kings will be forsaken.

target_units.text: The king of the Assyrians listened to him. The king of the Assyrians went up against Damascus, captured it, deported it, and put Raasson to death.

relationship: parallel Assyrian distress for Achaz's house
rationale: Isaiah announces trouble associated with the king of the Assyrians not experienced since Ephraim's removal from Judah; Chronicles describes Assour's king striking Ahaz and bringing no help despite gifts. Both turn Assyrian involvement into trouble for Judah's king.
source_text: But God will bring upon you, upon your people and upon your father’s house days that have not yet come since the day He removed Ephraim from Judah—the king of the Assyrians.”

target_units.text: Thaglath-phellasar king of Assour came against him and struck him.
Ahaz took what was in the Lord’s house, in the king’s house, and among the rulers, and gave it to Assour’s king, but it brought him no help.

relationship: related bee imagery for hostile military pursuit
rationale: Isaiah portrays the Assyrian force as a bee summoned by the Lord; Deuteronomy likens the Amorites' pursuit to bees. The insect image makes hostile pressure vivid in both, while the armies and events are distinct.
source_text: On that day the Lord will whistle for flies—what rules a part of Egypt’s river—and for the bee that is in the Assyrians’ country,

target_units.text: And the Amorites who dwelt in that hill country came out to meet you, and pursued you as bees do, and wounded you from Seir unto Hormah.

relationship: parallel shaving of head and beard as judgment imagery
rationale: Isaiah's great and drunken razor removes head hair and beard in an Assyrian judgment image; Ezekiel uses a sword sharper than a barber's razor to shave his head and beard for a siege sign. The target clarifies a comparable enacted judgment image without changing Isaiah's razor into a hired one.
source_text: On that day the Lord will shave with the great and drunken razor that is beyond the river of the king of the Assyrians—the head and the hair of the feet—and He will remove the beard.

target_units.text: “And you, son of man, take a sword sharper than a barber’s razor. Obtain it for yourself and pass it over your head and your beard. Take a balance with weights and divide the hairs;

burn a quarter with fire inside the city when the days of siege are complete. Take a quarter and burn it up in its midst; cut down a quarter with the sword around it, and scatter a quarter to the wind. I will draw a sword after them.
Take a few of them in number and gather them into your cloak.
Take some of these again, cast them into the fire, and burn them in the fire. From it fire will go out. And you will say to the entire house of Israel,

relationship: related provision of honey and dairy produce
rationale: Isaiah links abundant milk with the remaining inhabitants' diet of butter and honey; the song in Deuteronomy remembers God's provision of honey, butter of cattle, and milk of sheep. The specific foods correspond, while the historical settings differ.
source_text: and because they produce very much milk, everyone left upon the land will eat butter and honey.

target_units.text: He brought them up upon the strength of the earth, and fed them the produce of the fields; they sucked honey out of the rock, and oil out of the solid rock,
butter of cattle and milk of sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, young bulls and goats, with the fat of the kernels of wheat; and they drank wine, the blood of the grape.

relationship: related vineyard image of cultivation becoming wasteland
rationale: Isaiah's valuable vineyard becomes fallow ground and thorn; Proverbs compares a person lacking understanding to a vineyard that becomes abandoned wasteland if left alone. The shared ruined-cultivation image does not turn Proverbs' person-as-vineyard comparison into a literal vineyard visit.
source_text: On that day every place where there are a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels will become fallow ground and thorn.

target_units.text: A foolish man is like a cultivated field, and a person lacking understanding like a vineyard;
if you leave him alone, he will become wasteland, and grow wild with grass all over and become abandoned, and his stone fences are torn down.

relationship: related sheep and cattle imagery in transformed land
rationale: Isaiah 7 describes sheep pasture and cattle trampling ground emerging from fallow thorn-land; Isaiah 5 describes lambs feeding in deserted places and plundered people pastured like bulls. The pastoral imagery corresponds while preserving the figurative people in 5:17.
source_text: Every mountain that is plowed will be plowed, and fear will certainly not come there; for from fallow ground and thorn it will become pasture for sheep and a trampling place for cattle.

target_units.text: Those who were plundered will be pastured like bulls, and lambs will feed upon the deserted places of those wiped out.

relationship: parallel command to inscribe a prophetic message
rationale: Isaiah is told to write the approaching plunder message on a large new sheet; Habakkuk is told to write a vision clearly on a tablet, with its appointed realization in view. Both give a durable written form to an impending prophetic message.
source_text: The Lord said to me, “Take a large new sheet and write on it with a human stylus: ‘To make plunder of spoils swiftly; for it is at hand.’”

target_units.text: The Lord answered me: “Write a vision clearly on a boxwood tablet, so that the one reading these things may pursue them.
For the vision is still for a season, and it will rise toward the end and not toward emptiness. If he delays, wait for him, for coming he will come and certainly will not linger.

relationship: related witnessed prophetic documentation
rationale: Isaiah is told to appoint reliable witnesses for the written sign; Jeremiah writes and seals a purchase document before witnesses and orders its preservation as part of a prophetic transaction. The documents serve different purposes, but both use witnesses to attest a tangible prophetic act.
source_text: “Make reliable men witnesses for Me, Uriah and Zechariah son of Barachias.”

target_units.text: I wrote a document, sealed it, called witnesses, and weighed the silver on a balance.
I took the purchase document, the sealed one and the one that had been read.

I gave it to Baruch son of Neriah son of Maaseiah, before Hanamel my father’s brother’s son, before those standing there and writing in the purchase document, and before the Judeans in the prison court.
Before their eyes I instructed Baruch:
Thus said the Lord Almighty: Take this purchase document and the document that has been read, and put it in an earthenware vessel so that it may last many days.

relationship: parallel child given a divinely appointed judgment name
rationale: Isaiah's prophetess bears a son named by the Lord for approaching plunder; Hosea's wife bears a son whom the Lord names Jezreel in connection with impending judgment. Both turn a prophet's child's name into a public warning.
source_text: I approached the prophetess; she became pregnant and bore a son. The Lord said to me, “Call his name Plunder-quickly, Spoil-swiftly,

target_units.text: He went and took Gomer daughter of Debelaim; she conceived and bore him a son.
The Lord said to him, “Call him Jezreel, for in a little while I will avenge Jezreel’s blood upon Jehu’s house and put an end to the kingdom of Israel’s house.

relationship: historical counterpart to Assyrian seizure of Damascus
rationale: Isaiah names the removal of Damascus's power before Assyria's king; Kings narrates that king's capture of Damascus, deportation, and killing of Raasson. This supports the Damascus clause without claiming proof of the child's speech-development timetable or the Samaria clause.
source_text: because before the child knows how to call father or mother, he will take Damascus’s power and Samaria’s spoils before the king of the Assyrians.”

target_units.text: The king of the Assyrians listened to him. The king of the Assyrians went up against Damascus, captured it, deported it, and put Raasson to death.

relationship: parallel near political judgment attached to a child's sign-name
rationale: Isaiah connects the newborn sign with impending loss for Damascus and Samaria; Hosea's naming of Jezreel is followed by the announcement that Israel's kingdom and bow will be broken in a little while. The child-sign and near political judgment correspond, while the names and threatened events differ.
source_text: because before the child knows how to call father or mother, he will take Damascus’s power and Samaria’s spoils before the king of the Assyrians.”

target_units.text: The Lord said to him, “Call him Jezreel, for in a little while I will avenge Jezreel’s blood upon Jehu’s house and put an end to the kingdom of Israel’s house.
On that day I will shatter Israel’s bow in the Valley of Jezreel.”

relationship: related rejection expressed through water imagery
rationale: Isaiah describes rejection of quietly flowing Siloam in favor of Raasson and Romelias's son; Jeremiah depicts the people abandoning God, the spring of living water, for broken cisterns. Both expose a disastrous rejected source through water imagery; Jeremiah's explicit identification of the spring as God is not substituted into Isaiah's wording.
source_text: “Because this people does not want Siloam’s water, which flows quietly, but wants to have Raasson and Romelias’s son as king over you,

target_units.text: For My people did two evil things: they abandoned Me, a spring of water of life, and dug broken cisterns for themselves that will not be able to hold water.

relationship: parallel foreign power portrayed as an overwhelming river
rationale: Isaiah identifies the strong abundant river with Assyria's king; Jeremiah portrays Egypt rising like a river to cover the land and destroy its inhabitants. The inundating military image corresponds, while the foreign powers are different.
source_text: therefore, behold, the Lord brings up against you the river’s strong and abundant water—the king of the Assyrians and his glory. He will ascend every ravine of yours and walk over every wall of yours,

target_units.text: Who is this who will rise like a river, and like rivers churn water?
Egypt’s waters will rise like a river, and it said, I will rise and cover the land and destroy those living in it.
Mount the horses; prepare the chariots! Go out, warriors of the Ethiopians and Libyans equipped with weapons! And Lydians, go up and draw the bow!

relationship: later historical counterpart to Assyrian invasion of Judah
rationale: Isaiah describes Assyrian encampment filling Judah's breadth and removing its capable people; Kings records Sennacherib taking Judah's fortified cities under Hezekiah. This is a concrete historical counterpart to Assyrian penetration of Judah, not proof that every detail names that one campaign.
source_text: and he will remove from Judea a person able to lift a head or someone strong enough to accomplish anything. His encampment will fill the breadth of your country. God is with us.”

target_units.text: In King Hezekiah’s fourteenth year, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians went up against Judah’s fortified cities and captured them.

relationship: related warning to nations and rulers under God's power
rationale: Isaiah addresses nations and distant peoples whose renewed strength will still end in defeat; the psalm calls kings and judges to instruction and fear of the Lord lest His anger bring destruction. Both subordinate political strength to the Lord's authority.
source_text: Know, nations, and be defeated! Listen, you at the farthest edge of the earth! You who have grown strong, be defeated; for even if you grow strong again, you will again be defeated.

target_units.text: And now, kings, understand; be instructed, all who judge the earth.
Serve the Lord with fear, and exult in Him with trembling.
Take hold of instruction, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from a righteous way. When His fury burns quickly, blessed are all who have trusted in Him.

relationship: parallel scattering of political counsel by the Lord
rationale: Isaiah says the Lord will scatter whatever counsel the nations devise and their word will not endure; the psalm likewise says He scatters nations' counsels and nullifies rulers' plans while His own counsel remains.
source_text: Whatever counsel you devise, the Lord will scatter; whatever word you speak will certainly not endure for you, because the Lord God is with us.

target_units.text: The Lord scatters the counsels of nations; He nullifies the plans of peoples and nullifies the counsels of rulers.
But the Lord’s counsel remains for ever, the plans of His heart from generation to generation.

relationship: parallel confidence grounded in God being with His people
rationale: Isaiah grounds the failure of hostile counsel in God being with us; Paul asks who can stand against us if God is for us. The shared divine-presence argument supports confidence against opposition in different covenantal settings.
source_text: Whatever counsel you devise, the Lord will scatter; whatever word you speak will certainly not endure for you, because the Lord God is with us.

target_units.text: What, then, shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?

relationship: reuse of the command not to fear their fear
rationale: After Isaiah's difficult opening warning about what the people call hard, the verse says not to fear its fear or be troubled. First Peter repeats that latter command when addressing suffering for righteousness; it does not interpret the opening as a conspiracy saying.
source_text: ‘Never say hard; for everything this people says is hard.’ But do not fear its fear, and do not be troubled.

target_units.text: But even if you should suffer for righteousness, you are blessed. Do not fear their fear, and do not be troubled,

relationship: related command to sanctify the Lord
rationale: Isaiah commands sanctifying the Lord Himself as one's fear; First Peter commands sanctifying Christ as Lord in the heart. The latter explicitly applies the sanctifying command to Christ while adding the heart and readiness-to-answer setting.
source_text: Sanctify the Lord Himself, and He will be your fear.

target_units.text: but sanctify Christ as Lord in your hearts, always ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you for an account of the hope within you,

relationship: reuse of stumbling-stone language in a composite scriptural citation
rationale: Isaiah contrasts trusting sanctuary with encountering a stumbling stone or falling rock; Romans uses the stone of stumbling and rock of offense to explain Israel's stumbling because its pursuit was as though from works, not from faith. The citation develops the stone image without erasing Isaiah's protection for those who trust.
source_text: If you trust in Him, He will become a sanctuary for you, and you will not encounter Him as the stumbling of a stone or as the falling of a rock. But Jacob’s house is in a trap, and those settled in Jerusalem in a pit.

target_units.text: Why? Because it was not from faith, but as though from works. They stumbled against the stone of stumbling,
just as it is written, “Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, and the one who believes in Him will not be put to shame.”

relationship: Christological use of the stone and differing responses
rationale: First Peter applies the stone-of-stumbling wording to disobedience toward Christ, while distinguishing the honor of believers. Isaiah likewise distinguishes those trusting the Lord from the trapped house, though its supplied wording presents sanctuary and avoidance of stumbling conditionally.
source_text: If you trust in Him, He will become a sanctuary for you, and you will not encounter Him as the stumbling of a stone or as the falling of a rock. But Jacob’s house is in a trap, and those settled in Jerusalem in a pit.

target_units.text: For it stands in Scripture: “Look, I am laying in Zion a stone, a chosen, precious cornerstone, and the one who believes in Him will certainly not be put to shame.”
Therefore, the honor is for you who believe; but for those who do not believe, “The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner,”
and “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” They stumble, disobeying the word; to this they were also appointed.

relationship: related falling and breaking in the stone context
rationale: After Isaiah's rock-and-stumbling imagery, many fall and are broken; Jesus says that everyone falling upon the rejected stone will be shattered. The shared fall-and-break consequence links the adjacent stone contexts without identifying every group or event.
source_text: Therefore many among them will be powerless, fall and be broken; people who are secure will draw near and be captured.”

target_units.text: But He looked at them and said, “What, then, is this that is written: ‘The stone the builders rejected—this became the head of the corner’?
Everyone who falls upon that stone will be shattered; but whoever it falls upon, it will crush him.”

relationship: parallel exposure of obstructed access to divine instruction
rationale: Isaiah announces the revealing of those sealing the law so it may not be learned; Jesus condemns law experts for taking away the key of knowledge and hindering entry. Both expose people obstructing others' access to instruction, using different images.
source_text: Then those sealing up the law so that it may not be learned will be revealed.

target_units.text: Woe to you experts in the Law, because you have taken away the key of knowledge! You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.”

relationship: quotation of the declaration of trust
rationale: Hebrews quotes the declaration of trust immediately before quoting Isaiah's children saying, placing both in its argument about the Son and His brothers. The target matches Isaiah's trust clause, not the additional statement about God's hidden face.
source_text: He will say, “I will wait for God, who turned His face away from Jacob’s house, and I will put my trust in Him.”

target_units.text: And again, “I will put My trust in Him.” And again, “Behold, I and the children whom God gave Me.”

relationship: explicit quotation of the speaker and God-given children
rationale: Hebrews repeats 'I and the children whom God gave Me' within its account of the Son's solidarity with those He sanctifies. This directly takes up Isaiah's speaker-and-children sign language in a new stated application.
source_text: Behold, I and the children God gave me—and it will be for signs and wonders in Israel’s house, from the Lord Sabaoth, who dwells on Mount Zion.

target_units.text: And again, “I will put My trust in Him.” And again, “Behold, I and the children whom God gave Me.”

relationship: parallel rejection of consulting mediums and the dead
rationale: Isaiah challenges seeking belly-speakers and the dead concerning the living instead of turning to God; Deuteronomy prohibits mediums and inquiry of the dead among practices detestable to the Lord.
source_text: If they say to you, “Seek those who speak from the earth and the belly-speakers, the empty-talkers who speak from the belly,” should not a nation turn to its God? Why do they seek the dead concerning the living?

target_units.text: There shall not be found among you one who purifies his son or his daughter by fire, or practises divination, or interprets spoken omens, or observes auguries, or works sorcery,
or chants spells, or is a medium, or observes portents, or inquires of the dead.
For everyone who does these things is an abomination unto the Lord your God; for because of these abominations the Lord shall destroy them from before you.

relationship: narrative instance of seeking a medium instead of the Lord
rationale: Chronicles explains Saul's death by disobedience, inquiry through a spirit medium, and failure to seek the Lord. That concrete contrast corresponds to Isaiah's question why a people consults the dead instead of its God; Chronicles also expressly says Samuel answered Saul.
source_text: If they say to you, “Seek those who speak from the earth and the belly-speakers, the empty-talkers who speak from the belly,” should not a nation turn to its God? Why do they seek the dead concerning the living?

target_units.text: Saul died in the lawless acts he committed against the Lord, according to the Lord’s word, because he did not keep it; because Saul inquired through the spirit medium to seek counsel, and Samuel the prophet answered him.
He did not seek the Lord, and He killed him and turned the kingdom over to David son of Jesse.

relationship: parallel inescapable darkness in the judgment scene
rationale: Isaiah describes affliction, confinement, and darkness preventing sight; Amos warns that the Lord's day brings darkness without brightness and escape from one danger into another. The shared oppressive darkness expresses judgment rather than relief.
source_text: and they will look down to the earth, and behold, affliction and confinement and darkness, constricted perplexity and darkness so that they cannot see,

target_units.text: Woe to those desiring the Lord’s day! Why is this Lord’s day for you? It is darkness, not light,
as when someone flees from a lion and a bear falls upon him, then leaps into his house, braces his hands upon the wall, and a snake bites him.
Is not the Lord’s day darkness rather than light, gloom that has no brightness in it?

relationship: explicit geographical quotation applied to Jesus in Galilee
rationale: Matthew identifies Jesus' settlement in Capernaum with Isaiah's Zebulun, Naphtali, sea-way, beyond-Jordan, and Galilee-of-the-nations language. The quotation continues into the light saying, while the geographic phrases are those supplied here in Isaiah 8:23.
source_text: and the one in confinement will not remain perplexed for a time. “Do this first, do it quickly, country of Zebulun, land of Naphtali, way of the sea, and the rest who dwell by the sea and beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations, the regions of Judea.”

target_units.text: Leaving Nazareth, He came and settled in Capernaum beside the sea, in the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali,
so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled:
“Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations:
the people sitting in darkness saw a great light, and for those sitting in the region and shadow of death a light rose.”
